points.guide: Newton's universal law of gravitation as given by $F = G\dfrac{m_1m_2}{r^2}$ for bodies treated as point masses.
aims: State Newton's universal law of gravitation and use it to calculate the force between two point masses.
Explain what it means for gravity to be an inverse-square law.

slides.title: Newton's universal law of gravitation
bullets: Every mass attracts every other mass: gravity is always attractive
The force acts along the straight line joining the two point masses
It is proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation
The two masses pull on each other with forces of equal size and opposite direction (Newton's third law), however different the masses
Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces, yet it controls the motion of moons, planets and galaxies
slides.notes: Newton published the law in 1687, showing that the force that makes an apple fall also holds the Moon in its orbit. Ask why the weakest force rules astronomy: masses never cancel each other out, unlike positive and negative charges.

slides.title: The universal law of gravitation
bullets: $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-2}$, the universal gravitational constant
$r$ is the distance between the centres of the two masses
Inverse-square law: double $r$ and the force falls to a quarter
slides.notes: Both the law and G are in the data booklet. Henry Cavendish first measured G in 1798, with a torsion balance and large lead spheres; its tiny size is why we never notice the pull between everyday objects.

slides.title: Using the law: tips
bullets: Masses in kilograms and distances in metres
Remember to square the separation
For "what happens if…" questions, use proportion: $F \propto m_1m_2$ and $F \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$
On the calculator, find $Gm_1m_2$ and $r^{2}$ first, then divide

slides.title: A tabletop measurement
slides.question: Two lead spheres, each of mass 15 kg, sit with their centres 0.20 m apart, as in a modern version of Cavendish's experiment. Find the gravitational force between them, and compare it with the weight of one sphere.
slides.hint: Use the law of gravitation with $r$ measured between the centres. The weight of a sphere is $mg$.

steps.text: Substitute into the law of gravitation.

slides.notes: The pull between the spheres is about the weight of a 0.04 mg speck of dust, which is why Cavendish needed a very sensitive torsion balance shielded from draughts.

slides.title: The Sun and Jupiter
slides.question: The Sun has a mass of $1.99 \times 10^{30}$ kg and Jupiter a mass of $1.90 \times 10^{27}$ kg. Their centres are $7.78 \times 10^{11}$ m apart on average. Find (a) the gravitational force between them and (b) the force if their separation were halved.
slides.hint: Work out the top and the bottom of the fraction separately. For (b), how does the force depend on the separation?
slides.notes: Jupiter pulls on the Sun with the same force. This makes the Sun wobble slightly around their common centre of mass, the effect astronomers use to detect planets around other stars.

points.guide: Conditions under which extended bodies can be treated as point masses.
aims: Explain when an extended body can be treated as a point mass, and measure separations between centres.

slides.title: When can a body be treated as a point?
bullets: Newton's law is written for point masses, but real bodies have size
A uniform sphere, or one made of uniform spherical layers like a planet, attracts objects outside it as if all its mass were at its centre
Any body can be treated as a point when it is tiny compared with the separation (a planet seen from the Sun)
So $r$ is measured centre to centre, never surface to surface
Two irregular bodies close together (two people side by side) can't be treated this simply
slides.notes: The guide extends the law to spheres of uniform density by treating their mass as concentrated at the centre. Newton proved this result, now called the shell theorem, in the Principia (1687).

slides.title: Two bowling balls
slides.question: Two bowling balls, each a uniform sphere of mass 7.0 kg and radius 0.11 m, rest touching each other. Find the gravitational force between them.
slides.hint: Treat each ball as a point mass at its centre. How far apart are the centres when the balls touch?

steps.text: The centres are two radii apart.
Substitute into the law of gravitation.

slides.notes: Ask why the answer isn't enormous even though the surfaces touch: the separation between centres can never be smaller than the sum of the radii.

points.guide: That gravitational field strength $g$ at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by $g = \dfrac{F}{m} = G\dfrac{M}{r^2}$.
aims: Define gravitational field strength and calculate it at and above the surface of a planet.
Use field strength to find weights and the masses of planets.

slides.title: Gravitational fields
bullets: A mass sets up a gravitational field around itself: a region in which any other mass feels a force
Gravitational field strength $g$: the force per unit mass on a small test mass placed at that point
The test mass is small so that it doesn't disturb the field it measures
Unit $\text{N kg}^{-1}$, the same as $\text{m s}^{-2}$: the field strength equals the free-fall acceleration
$g$ is a vector, pointing towards the mass that creates the field
slides.notes: The field picture replaces "action at a distance": the mass sets up a field in the space around it, and another mass responds to the field where it is. Weight, $F = mg$, is the force of the field on a mass.

slides.title: Field strength of a point or spherical mass
bullets: $M$ is the mass creating the field, and $r$ is measured from its centre
At the Earth's surface, $g = 9.8\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$

slides.title: Deriving the field strength of a planet
slides.start: A small mass $m$ is a distance $r$ from the centre of a planet of mass $M$. Newton's law gives the force on it, and the definition of field strength does the rest.

steps.text: The gravitational force on the small mass
Field strength is force per unit mass
At the surface, $r$ is the planet's radius $R$

slides.notes: Because m cancels, every object at the same place has the same free-fall acceleration, whatever its mass: Newton's law explains Galileo's observation.

slides.title: Using field strength: tips
bullets: Distance from the centre = the planet's radius + the height above the surface
Outside a planet $g \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$: at twice the distance from the centre, a quarter of the surface value
Weight anywhere is $mg$, with the local value of $g$
Rearranged, $M = \dfrac{gR^{2}}{G}$ gives a planet's mass from its surface field strength and radius

slides.title: How field strength falls with distance
On the surface of Venus
slides.question: The mass of Venus is $4.87 \times 10^{24}$ kg, and its radius is $6.05 \times 10^{6}$ m. Find the gravitational field strength at its surface, and the weight there of a 1.5 kg rock sample.
slides.hint: Use $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}$ with the radius of Venus. Then weight = mass × field strength.
slides.notes: Venus is almost the Earth's twin in size and mass, so its surface field is about 90% of ours.

slides.title: A navigation satellite
slides.question: A navigation satellite of mass 1630 kg orbits $2.66 \times 10^{7}$ m from the Earth's centre. The Earth's radius is $6.37 \times 10^{6}$ m and the field strength at its surface is $9.8\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$. Find (a) the gravitational field strength at the satellite and (b) the satellite's weight there.
slides.hint: Outside the Earth, $g \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$ with $r$ from the centre. Compare the satellite's distance with the Earth's radius.
slides.notes: The ratio method needs no value for G or the Earth's mass. Gravity is still there in orbit: about 6% of its surface value at this distance.

slides.title: Weighing Mercury
slides.question: The gravitational field strength at the surface of Mercury is $3.7\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$, and Mercury's radius is $2.44 \times 10^{6}$ m. Deduce the mass of Mercury.
slides.hint: Rearrange $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}$ to make $M$ the subject.
slides.notes: In practice, planetary masses are found from the orbits of moons and space probes, using the same law of gravitation.

aims: Sketch and interpret gravitational field lines for radial and uniform fields.
Find the resultant gravitational field strength at points on the line joining two bodies.

slides.title: Gravitational field lines
bullets: A field line shows the direction of the force on a small test mass
Gravitational field lines point towards the mass, because gravity only attracts
The closer together the lines, the stronger the field
Field lines never cross: the field has only one direction at each point
Around a planet the field is radial; over a small region near its surface it is almost uniform
slides.notes: The guide requires sketching and interpreting field lines. Ask students why the field over a classroom is drawn as parallel lines when the Earth is round.

slides.title: The field of two bodies
bullets: Field strength is a vector, so the fields of two bodies add as vectors
On the line between two masses, the two fields point in opposite directions and partly cancel
At one point between them the resultant field is zero; it is nearer the smaller mass
Beyond either mass, on the same line, the two fields point the same way and add
IB calculations are limited to points on the line joining the two bodies

slides.title: Two fields at one point
bullets: Choose a positive direction along the line
Measure each distance from the centre of that body
Give each field a sign, then add

slides.title: Pluto and Charon
slides.question: Pluto (mass $1.30 \times 10^{22}$ kg) and its moon Charon (mass $1.59 \times 10^{21}$ kg) have centres $1.96 \times 10^{7}$ m apart. Find the distance from Pluto's centre to the point between them where the resultant gravitational field strength is zero.
slides.hint: Call the distance from Pluto $x$, so the distance from Charon is $d - x$. Set the two field strengths equal; taking square roots avoids a quadratic.

steps.text: Set the two field strengths equal ($G$ cancels).
Take the square root of both sides.

slides.notes: Check: the point is nearer Charon, the smaller mass. Charon is unusually large for a moon, so the point is only about three quarters of the way across.

slides.title: A probe between the Earth and the Sun
slides.question: A space probe is on the line between the Earth and the Sun, $1.0 \times 10^{9}$ m from the Earth's centre. The Sun's mass is $1.99 \times 10^{30}$ kg, the Earth's is $5.97 \times 10^{24}$ kg, and the Earth–Sun distance is $1.50 \times 10^{11}$ m. Determine the resultant gravitational field strength at the probe.
slides.hint: Find each field strength separately, with each distance measured from that body's centre. Do the two fields point the same way or opposite ways?

steps.text: The Earth's field, $GM_{E}/r^{2}$, towards the Earth.
The probe's distance from the Sun.
The Sun's field, $GM_{S}/r_{S}^{2}$, towards the Sun.
The fields are opposite, so subtract: the resultant points towards the Sun.

slides.notes: Even about 2.6 times as far away as the Moon, the Sun's field at the probe is 15 times stronger than the Earth's.

points.guide: Kepler's three laws of orbital motion.
aims: State Kepler's three laws of orbital motion.
Deduce Kepler's third law for a circular orbit, and use it to find periods, orbital radii and central masses.

slides.title: Orbits: gravity as the centripetal force
bullets: A satellite in a circular orbit is in free fall: it falls towards the planet, but moves sideways fast enough to keep missing it
The gravitational force provides the centripetal force (A.2)
The satellite's own mass cancels, so every body at the same orbital radius has the same speed and period
In IB calculations, orbits are treated as circles
slides.notes: Newton's cannonball thought experiment works well here: fire a ball horizontally from a very high mountain, faster each time, until the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls.

slides.title: Weightlessness in orbit
bullets: Astronauts in orbit are still in the Earth's field: 400 km up, $g$ is about 90% of its value at the surface
The astronauts and their spacecraft are in free fall together, all with the same acceleration
Nothing pushes on them, so they feel weightless, but their weight is not zero
In a lift accelerating upwards at $a$, a dropped ball seems to fall at $g + a$; accelerating downwards, at $g - a$
Only far from every mass, in deep space, is a body truly weightless
slides.notes: If the lift's acceleration downwards equals g (the cable snaps), a dropped ball seems to float: the same situation as in orbit. Aircraft flying parabolic paths give astronauts about 20 seconds of free fall at a time for training.

slides.title: Kepler's three laws
bullets: First law: the orbit of every planet is an ellipse, with the Sun at one of its two foci
Second law: a line joining the Sun and a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals, so the planet moves fastest when nearest the Sun
Third law: $T^{2} \propto r^{3}$, where $T$ is the period and $r$ the mean radius of the orbit
Kepler found these patterns in Tycho Brahe's observations; Newton's law of gravitation later explained them
slides.notes: Real planetary orbits are close to circles: the Earth's distance from the Sun varies by only about 3% over a year. The laws apply equally to moons and satellites orbiting a much larger mass.

slides.title: Kepler's third law for a circular orbit
bullets: $M$ is the mass being orbited; the orbiting body's mass does not appear
For all bodies orbiting the same mass, $\dfrac{T^{2}}{r^{3}}$ has the same value
Not in the data booklet: deduce it
slides.notes: New for exams from 2028. The derivation on the next slide is now expected of all students, SL and HL.

slides.title: Deducing Kepler's third law
slides.start: A body of mass $m$ moves in a circular orbit of radius $r$, with period $T$, around a much larger mass $M$. Gravity provides the centripetal force.

steps.text: One orbit, of length $2\pi r$, takes a time $T$

slides.notes: New for exams from 2028. The 2028 guide says all students should be able to deduce Kepler's third law from the centripetal and gravitational force relationships for circular orbits. Kepler knew only that T² ∝ r³; Newton's law also gives the constant, 4π²/GM.

slides.title: Using Kepler's third law: tips
bullets: Use the period in seconds and the radius in metres, measured from the centre of the mass being orbited
For two bodies orbiting the same mass, use ratios: $\left(\dfrac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}\right)^{2} = \left(\dfrac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}\right)^{3}$, in any consistent units
Rearranged, $M = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}r^{3}}{GT^{2}}$ gives the central mass from a single orbit
A larger orbit always has a longer period

slides.title: Weighing the Sun
slides.question: The Earth orbits the Sun at a mean radius of $1.50 \times 10^{11}$ m, taking 365 days. Treating the orbit as a circle, determine the mass of the Sun.
slides.hint: Convert the period to seconds, then rearrange Kepler's third law to make $M$ the subject.

steps.text: Work out the top of the fraction.

slides.notes: The same method gives the mass of any planet that has a moon, and the mass of the black hole at the centre of our galaxy from the orbits of the stars close to it.

slides.title: Saturn's year
slides.question: Saturn orbits the Sun at 9.54 times the Earth's orbital radius. Treating both orbits as circles, find the length of Saturn's year in Earth years.
slides.hint: Both planets orbit the same mass, so compare them with a ratio. The units cancel, so years and Earth orbital radii can be used directly.

steps.text: Kepler's third law as a ratio.

slides.notes: Saturn is a little under ten times as far from the Sun as we are, but its year is nearly thirty times as long: it travels a longer path, more slowly.

slides.title: The Hubble Space Telescope
slides.question: The Hubble Space Telescope orbits about 540 km above the Earth's surface. The Earth's mass is $5.97 \times 10^{24}$ kg and its radius is $6.37 \times 10^{6}$ m. Find the period of the telescope's orbit, in minutes.
slides.hint: Add the height to the Earth's radius to get the orbital radius. Then use Kepler's third law.

steps.text: Add the height, $5.4 \times 10^{5}$ m, to the Earth's radius.

slides.notes: All satellites a few hundred kilometres up take about an hour and a half per orbit, so astronauts see about 15 sunrises a day.

points.guide: That the gravitational potential energy $E_p$ of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of the components of the system.
aims: Define gravitational potential energy as the work done to assemble a system from infinite separation.
Explain why gravitational potential energy is negative, with zero at infinite separation.

slides.title: Gravity is a conservative force
bullets: The work done by gravity on a mass moving between two points does not depend on the path taken
Such forces are called conservative; friction is not (a longer path means more work against it)
Only conservative forces have a potential energy
Near the ground, $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$ assumes a constant $g$ and uses a zero we choose
slides.notes: The next slide shows why the path doesn't matter, using a straight path and a staircase path.

slides.title: Two paths from A to B
slides.alt: Two paths from point A up to point B, which is a height h higher. One is a straight slope. The other is a staircase with three vertical steps, h1, h2 and h3, joined by horizontal steps. A mass on the slope has its weight mg drawn straight down.
bullets: Both paths start at A and end at B, a height $h$ higher
Gravity does work only on the vertical parts of a path
The vertical steps add up: $h_1 + h_2 + h_3 = h$

slides.title: Gravity does the same work on any path
slides.start: A mass $m$ is moved from A to B, a height $h$ higher: first along a straight slope, then by a staircase path with vertical steps $h_1$, $h_2$, $h_3$ and horizontal steps between them.

steps.text: Along the slope, the displacement's component along the line of the force is $h$, against the force
Horizontal steps: the force is at right angles to the displacement
The vertical steps add up to the same height, so the work is the same

slides.notes: Any path can be split into tiny vertical and horizontal steps, so the result holds for every path. Contrast friction: dragging a box along a longer route takes more work.

slides.title: Potential energy of a system
bullets: Gravitational potential energy belongs to a system of masses, not to one mass on its own
Its zero is at infinite separation, where the masses no longer interact
$E_p$ is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation
The masses attract, so they come together without any push: the work done to assemble them is negative
So $E_p$ is negative at every finite separation, and increases towards zero as the masses move apart
slides.notes: Students often find negative energy strange. A system with negative potential energy is bound: energy must be supplied to pull it apart.

slides.title: A meteoroid arrives
slides.question: A meteoroid starts at rest very far from the Earth and falls towards it. Describe and explain how the gravitational potential energy of the Earth–meteoroid system changes, and where the energy goes.
slides.hint: Where is the potential energy zero? Does gravity do positive or negative work as the separation decreases?

steps.text: Very far away the separation is effectively infinite, so the potential energy starts at zero.
As the meteoroid falls, gravity does positive work on it, so the system's potential energy decreases: it becomes negative.
The energy lost from the potential energy becomes kinetic energy of the meteoroid (ignoring air resistance).
The closer it gets, the more negative the potential energy and the faster the meteoroid moves.

slides.notes: Reversing the process, external work equal to the size of the potential energy would be needed to separate the Earth and the meteoroid again.

points.guide: The gravitational potential energy for a two-body system as given by $E_p = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r}$ where $r$ is the separation between the centre of mass of the two bodies.
aims: Calculate the gravitational potential energy of a two-body system, and changes in it.

slides.title: Potential energy of two masses
bullets: $r$ is the separation between the centres of the two bodies
Note the minus sign, and that $r$ is not squared
From $r_1$ to $r_2$: $\Delta E_p = Gm_1m_2\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)$
slides.notes: In the data booklet. The change formula comes from subtracting the two values of $E_p$; it is positive when $r_2 > r_1$.

slides.title: Using the formula: tips
bullets: Keep the minus sign: moving apart makes $E_p$ less negative, so it increases
Doubling the separation halves the size of $E_p$: it varies as $\dfrac{1}{r}$, not $\dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$
For small height changes near a surface, $mg\Delta h$ is a good approximation; for large ones it is not, because $g$ changes

slides.title: The Sun–Earth system
slides.question: The Sun's mass is $1.99 \times 10^{30}$ kg, the Earth's is $5.97 \times 10^{24}$ kg, and their separation is $1.50 \times 10^{11}$ m. Find (a) the gravitational potential energy of the Sun–Earth system and (b) the minimum work needed to separate them completely if both started at rest.
slides.hint: Use $E_p = -\dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r}$. For (b), what is the potential energy once they are infinitely far apart?

steps.text: Divide by the separation and keep the minus sign.
(b) At infinite separation $E_p = 0$, so the work needed is

slides.notes: The real Earth is moving, and its kinetic energy is half the size of $E_p$ (see orbital energy), so only about $2.6 \times 10^{33}$ J would be needed in practice.

points.guide: That the gravitational potential $V_g$ at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point as given by $V_g = -\dfrac{GM}{r}$.
aims: Define gravitational potential, and calculate it for one or more masses.

slides.title: Gravitational potential
bullets: Gravitational potential $V_g$ at a point: the work needed per kilogram to bring a small test mass there from infinity
It describes the field itself, whatever mass is placed there: $E_p = mV_g$
Unit $\text{J kg}^{-1}$
It is a scalar, so the potentials of several masses simply add
Zero at infinity, and negative everywhere else
slides.notes: Potential and potential energy are easily confused: potential is the energy per kilogram, a property of a point in the field.

slides.title: Potential of a point or spherical mass
bullets: $r$ is measured from the centre of the mass (outside a spherical body)
Most negative at the surface, rising towards zero far away

slides.title: From potential energy to potential
slides.start: A small mass $m$ is a distance $r$ from the centre of a mass $M$. Potential is potential energy per unit mass.

steps.text: Potential energy of the two-body system
Potential is energy per unit mass

slides.title: Using potential: tips
bullets: Add potentials as numbers, including their minus signs: no directions needed
Use $E_p = mV_g$ for the potential energy of a mass at a point
Don't confuse $V_g \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$ with $g \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$

slides.title: Halfway between Pluto and Charon
slides.question: Pluto (mass $1.30 \times 10^{22}$ kg) and Charon (mass $1.59 \times 10^{21}$ kg) have centres $1.96 \times 10^{7}$ m apart. Find (a) the gravitational potential at the midpoint between them and (b) the gravitational potential energy of a 400 kg probe placed there.
slides.hint: Each body contributes its own potential, and potentials are scalars. How far is the midpoint from each centre?

steps.text: The midpoint is half the separation from each centre.

slides.notes: At the midpoint the two fields point in opposite directions and partly cancel, but the two potentials add: one is a vector, the other a scalar.

points.short: Work done in a gravitational field
points.guide: The work done in moving a mass $m$ in a gravitational field as given by $W = m\Delta V_g$.
aims: Calculate the work done in moving a mass between two points in a gravitational field.

slides.title: Work done moving a mass
bullets: $\Delta V_g$ = final potential − initial potential
Moving away from a planet, $\Delta V_g$ is positive: work must be done on the mass
The work depends only on the start and end points, not on the path
slides.notes: In the data booklet. This is the minimum work, with the mass at rest at the start and the end.

slides.title: Work in a field: tips
bullets: Find the potential at each point with $V_g = -\dfrac{GM}{r}$, using distances from the centre
Or in one step: $\Delta V_g = GM\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)$
Moving along an equipotential needs no work, since $\Delta V_g = 0$
Use $mg\Delta h$ only when the height change is small compared with the planet's radius

slides.title: Leaving the Moon
slides.question: A 600 kg lunar probe is lifted from the Moon's surface to a height of 100 km. The Moon's mass is $7.35 \times 10^{22}$ kg and its radius is $1.74 \times 10^{6}$ m. Find (a) the work done against gravity and (b) the percentage error if $mg\Delta h$ were used with $g = 1.62\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$.
slides.hint: Find the distance from the Moon's centre at 100 km, then the change in potential. Why should $mg\Delta h$ give a slightly larger answer?

steps.text: Distance from the centre, 100 km up.
About 6% too large, because $g$ weakens with height.

slides.notes: The 100 km climb is about 6% of the Moon's radius, and the error is about the same size: a quick way to judge whether $mg\Delta h$ is good enough.

points.guide: The gravitational field strength $g$ as the gravitational potential gradient as given by $g = -\dfrac{\Delta V_g}{\Delta r}$.
aims: Relate field strength to potential gradient, and find $g$ from potential values or from the gradient of a graph of $V_g$ against $r$.

slides.title: Field strength and potential gradient
bullets: The potential gradient is the change in potential per unit distance, $\dfrac{\Delta V_g}{\Delta r}$
Field strength = −(potential gradient)
The minus sign: the field points towards lower potential, inwards towards the mass
Units: $\text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{m}^{-1} = \text{N kg}^{-1}$, since 1 J = 1 N m
The field strength at a point is minus the gradient of the tangent to a $V_g$–$r$ graph there

slides.title: The potential gradient
bullets: In the data booklet
Over a large $\Delta r$ this gives an average field strength; for a value at one point, use a tangent

slides.title: Field strength from potential
slides.start: Near a planet's surface the field is uniform, with strength $g$. A mass $m$ is raised at constant speed through a small height $\Delta r$, against its weight $mg$.

steps.text: The same work, in terms of potential
The potential rises outwards, but the field points inwards: the minus sign shows the direction

slides.notes: In steps 1–3, g is the size of the field. In the final form, g is the field component in the direction of increasing r, which is negative because the field points inwards. The result holds in any field, taking a small Δr.

slides.title: Field strength from a potential graph
Two potential readings
slides.question: Two points on a line out from a planet's centre are $8.0 \times 10^{6}$ m and $8.2 \times 10^{6}$ m from the centre. The gravitational potentials there are $-5.00 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$ and $-4.88 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$. Estimate the gravitational field strength between the two points.
slides.hint: Find the change in potential and the change in distance, both going outwards. Then use the potential gradient, keeping its sign.

steps.text: Potential gradient, with its minus sign.
The minus sign means the field points inwards: $6.0\ \text{N kg}^{-1}$ towards the planet.

slides.notes: This is an average over the interval. For this planet $GM = 4.0 \times 10^{14}$, and $GM/r^{2}$ at the midpoint gives 6.1 N kg⁻¹, which agrees.

aims: Describe and sketch equipotential surfaces around a planet and in a uniform field.

slides.title: Equipotential surfaces
bullets: An equipotential surface joins points with the same gravitational potential
Around a point or spherical mass: concentric spheres centred on the mass
Close to a planet's surface (uniform field): horizontal planes, equally spaced for equal steps of potential
Moving a mass along an equipotential needs no work, since $\Delta V_g = 0$
Drawn at equal steps of potential, they get further apart as the field weakens
slides.notes: Contour lines on a map are a good analogy: near the surface each contour is a line of equal height, and so of equal potential, because $\Delta V_g = g\Delta h$.

slides.title: Equipotentials around the Earth
slides.question: Equipotential surfaces are drawn around the Earth at $-6.0 \times 10^{7}$, $-5.0 \times 10^{7}$ and $-4.0 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}$. For the Earth, $GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-1}$. Find the radius of each surface, and show that the surfaces get further apart.
slides.hint: Rearrange $V_g = -\dfrac{GM}{r}$ to make $r$ the subject, then find the gaps between the surfaces.

steps.text: The gaps grow, though the steps in potential are equal.

slides.notes: The innermost surface is only about 260 km above the ground, since the Earth's radius is $6.37 \times 10^{6}$ m.

points.guide: The relationship between equipotential surfaces and gravitational field lines.
aims: Explain why field lines cross equipotential surfaces at right angles, and sketch both for one or two masses.

slides.title: Field lines and equipotentials
bullets: Field lines always cross equipotential surfaces at right angles
Reason: moving along an equipotential needs no work, so the field has no component along it
Field lines point from higher to lower potential
Where equipotentials (at equal steps) are closer together, the field is stronger
So either one can be sketched from the other: draw lines perpendicular to them everywhere
slides.notes: The guide asks students to be able to map fields using potential. Students can sketch field lines first, then equipotentials crossing them at right angles, or the other way round.

slides.title: Two masses
bullets: Between two masses there is a point where the resultant field is zero
There the potential along the line is at a maximum (least negative), so its gradient is zero
The potential there is not zero: both masses contribute negative potentials
Far from the pair, the equipotentials become spheres, as if the two were a single mass
slides.notes: A 3D "rubber sheet" picture of potential shows two pits with a saddle between them; the saddle point is where the field is zero.

slides.title: Two equal masses
slides.alt: Two equal masses. Blue field lines curve in towards each mass from all directions. Orange dashed equipotentials form small loops around each mass and larger peanut-shaped loops around both. Midway between the masses, field lines from the two sides meet at a point marked g equals 0.
bullets: Blue: field lines, pointing towards the masses
Orange, dashed: equipotentials, crossing the field lines at right angles
Midway between the masses, $g = 0$
slides.notes: Calculated from the two masses' potentials. Far from the pair, the equipotentials become circles round both.

slides.title: Zero field, but not zero potential
slides.question: Two identical stars, each of mass $M$, are a distance $d$ apart. At the midpoint between them, find (a) the resultant gravitational field strength and (b) the gravitational potential, and (c) explain how both answers fit with $g = -\dfrac{\Delta V_g}{\Delta r}$.
slides.hint: Field strength is a vector and potential is a scalar. How do the two contributions combine in each case?

steps.text: (a) The two fields are equal in size and opposite in direction.
(b) Each star is $d/2$ away, and the scalar potentials add.
(c) Along the line, the potential is least negative at the midpoint, so its gradient there is zero: $g = 0$ although $V_g$ is not.

points.guide: The escape speed $v_{\text{esc}}$ at any point in a gravitational field as given by $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2GM}{r}}$.
aims: Derive the escape speed from energy conservation, and use it at a planet's surface and in orbit.

slides.title: Escape speed
bullets: The escape speed at a point: the minimum speed an object needs there to reach infinity, with no further energy input
It would arrive at infinity with zero speed and zero potential energy, so its total energy must be zero
It does not depend on the object's mass, or (ignoring air resistance) on the direction of launch
It applies at any point in the field, not only at the surface
slides.notes: Escape speed is for an unpowered object. A rocket whose engines keep firing can leave the Earth more slowly.

slides.title: Escape speed
bullets: In the data booklet
$r$ is the distance from the centre of the mass $M$

slides.title: Deriving the escape speed
slides.start: An object of mass $m$ is a distance $r$ from the centre of a mass $M$, moving at the escape speed. It just reaches infinity, where it comes to rest.
slides.notes: The derivation ignores air resistance and the planet's rotation, and treats the object as moving only under gravity once launched.

slides.title: Leaving Mars
slides.question: Find the escape speed from the surface of Mars, whose mass is $6.42 \times 10^{23}$ kg and radius $3.39 \times 10^{6}$ m.
slides.hint: Use the escape speed equation with $r$ equal to the radius of Mars. Find $GM$ first.

steps.text: Substitute into the escape speed equation.

slides.notes: This is about 45% of the Earth's escape speed, so each kilogram needs only about a fifth of the energy to leave Mars as to leave the Earth.

slides.title: Escaping from lunar orbit
slides.question: A spacecraft is in a circular orbit 100 km above the Moon's surface. The Moon's mass is $7.35 \times 10^{22}$ kg and its radius is $1.74 \times 10^{6}$ m. Find (a) the spacecraft's orbital speed, $\sqrt{GM/r}$, (b) the escape speed at that height and (c) the increase in speed it needs to escape from the Moon.
slides.hint: Use the same $r$, measured from the Moon's centre, in both equations. The increase is the difference between the two speeds.

steps.text: Orbital radius, from the Moon's centre ($GM = 4.90 \times 10^{12}$ for the Moon).
(b) Escape speed at the same radius.

slides.notes: At any radius the escape speed is √2 times the orbital speed. The extra speed is given by a short engine burn in the direction of motion: this is how missions left lunar orbit to return to the Earth.

points.guide: The orbital speed $v_{\text{orbital}}$ of a body orbiting a large mass as given by $v_{\text{orbital}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$.
aims: Derive the orbital speed, and the kinetic, potential and total energy of a satellite in a circular orbit.
Calculate the energy needed to launch a satellite into orbit and to change its orbit.

slides.title: Orbital speed
bullets: In the data booklet
It does not depend on the satellite's mass
A higher orbit is slower

slides.title: Deriving the orbital speed
slides.start: A satellite of mass $m$ is in a circular orbit of radius $r$ around a mass $M$.

slides.title: Deriving the energies of an orbit

steps.text: Potential energy of the satellite–planet system

slides.notes: So for every circular orbit, $E_k = -\tfrac{1}{2}E_p$ and $E = -E_k$. These results are not in the data booklet, so students should be able to derive them.

slides.title: Orbital energy: tips
bullets: A higher orbit has less kinetic energy, but more potential energy and more total energy (less negative)
Energy to move between circular orbits: $\Delta E = \dfrac{GMm}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_2}\right)$
Launch from a non-rotating planet: energy needed = $E$ in orbit − $\left(-\dfrac{GMm}{R}\right)$ on the surface
An orbiting satellite escapes if its total energy is raised to zero

slides.title: Energies of a satellite in orbit
A navigation satellite's energy
slides.question: A navigation satellite of mass 1630 kg is in a circular orbit of radius $2.66 \times 10^{7}$ m around the Earth ($GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-1}$). Find (a) its orbital speed and (b) its kinetic energy, the potential energy of the satellite–Earth system and the total energy.
slides.hint: Find the kinetic energy from $\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$. How are the potential and total energies related to it for a circular orbit?

steps.text: Potential energy: twice the size, negative.

slides.notes: Check (a) with the period: 2πr/v gives about 4.3 × 10⁴ s, roughly 12 hours, the real period of GPS satellites.

slides.title: Raising an orbit
slides.question: A 3500 kg satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius $7.0 \times 10^{6}$ m to one of radius $7.5 \times 10^{6}$ m around the Earth ($GM = 3.98 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\,\text{kg}^{-1}$). Find (a) the energy that must be supplied and (b) the change in its kinetic energy.
slides.hint: Compare the total energy, $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$, in the two orbits. For (b), how is the kinetic energy related to the total energy?

steps.text: (b) In a circular orbit $E_k = -E$, so the kinetic energy falls by the same amount.

slides.notes: The engines supply 6.6 GJ, yet the satellite ends up slower: the potential energy rises by 13 GJ, twice the energy supplied.

slides.title: From the surface of Mars into orbit
slides.question: An 800 kg probe is launched from the surface of Mars into a circular orbit 400 km above the surface. Mars: mass $6.42 \times 10^{23}$ kg, radius $3.39 \times 10^{6}$ m; treat it as not rotating. Find the minimum energy needed.
slides.hint: Resting on the surface, the probe has only potential energy. Once in orbit, its total energy is $-\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$: subtract one from the other.

steps.text: Add the height, $4.0 \times 10^{5}$ m, to the radius of Mars.
Energy at rest on the surface.

slides.notes: A real launch needs much more, because of the fuel that must itself be lifted and the energy lost to the thin atmosphere. A rotating planet gives a launch from the equator a head start.

points.guide: The qualitative effect of a small viscous drag force due to the atmosphere on the height and speed of an orbiting body.
aims: Explain how atmospheric drag changes the height, speed and energy of a satellite in a low orbit.

slides.title: Orbital decay
bullets: Satellites in low orbits move through the very thin upper atmosphere
A small viscous drag force does negative work on them, transferring energy to thermal energy
The total energy $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ becomes more negative, so the orbital radius decreases
In the lower orbit $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{GM}{r}}$ is larger: drag makes the satellite speed up
The air gets denser lower down, so the decay speeds up until the satellite re-enters and burns up
slides.notes: For every joule taken by drag, the potential energy falls by 2 J and the kinetic energy rises by 1 J, because $E_k = -E$ and $E_p = 2E$. The orbit stays almost circular because the drag is so small.

slides.title: A decaying orbit
slides.question: A small satellite in a low circular orbit loses 1.0 MJ of energy to air resistance over a month, while its orbit stays nearly circular. State and explain the changes in (a) its total energy, (b) its kinetic energy, (c) the gravitational potential energy and (d) its orbital radius.
slides.hint: Use the relationships between the energies of a circular orbit: how are $E_k$ and $E_p$ related to the total energy $E$?

steps.text: (a) Drag transfers energy away from the satellite.
(d) $E = -\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ is more negative, so $r$ is smaller: the satellite has dropped into a lower, faster orbit.

slides.notes: This is why satellites in low orbits, such as the space station, carry fuel to boost themselves back up from time to time.
